outcome: Jineon Baek's arXiv preprint 'Optimality of Gerver's Sofa' (arXiv:2411.19826, v1 posted 29 Nov 2024) claims that Gerver's 1992 sofa, of area about 2.2195, is the maximal-area moving sofa, which would settle the problem's value; no journal acceptance and no named human verification were found as of 13 Oct 2026, but three Lean 4 formalisations posted in Sep-Oct 2026 check the argument, two of them credit AI coding agents or models with the formalisation, and the two AI-credited repositories and an automated AI referee each report gaps or errors in the paper, one of them repaired.
problem_asks: (a) The largest area of a moving sofa: a planar rigid shape that can be moved by a continuous rotation and translation around the right-angled corner of an L-shaped hallway with legs of unit width. The statement asks for the value of this maximal area (the sofa constant). (b) It does not ask which shape attains the maximum, whether the maximiser is unique, or whether the maximum is stable under perturbation. Answering (a) exactly would settle the bullet; a bound moves the quantity asked for but does not give its value.

events.what_happened: J. M. Hammersley, Bulletin of the Institute of Mathematics and Its Applications 4 (1968) 66-85, Appendix IV, Problem 8 (reference as cited on the Wikipedia article): introduced a 'telephone-handset' shaped sofa of area pi/2 + 2/pi, about 2.2074, and gave the upper bound 2 sqrt(2), about 2.8284, for the sofa constant. The upper bound is taken from secondary sources (search snippets); the 1968 paper itself was not opened.
events.delivers: Lower bound about 2.2074 and upper bound about 2.8284 on the maximal area in the planar unit-width L-corridor.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks: the exact value, the maximiser, uniqueness and stability.
events.time_since_posted: Not assessed for this pre-window event.
events.direction: Bounds only; neither confirms nor refutes an optimality value.
events.object: Hammersley's telephone-handset-shaped sofa: explicit, area pi/2 + 2/pi (about 2.2074). Gerver later improved this shape to about 2.2195.

events.what_happened: J. L. Gerver, 'On moving a sofa around a corner', Geometriae Dedicata 42(3) (1992) 267-283 (reference as cited on the Wikipedia article). Gave a curved sofa with 18 curve sections, area about 2.2195, which is the leading lower bound and the conjectured optimum. Gerver showed local optimality only, not global optimality, per Wikipedia and the Quanta article. The 1992 paper itself was not opened.
events.delivers: Lower bound about 2.2195 on the maximal area, and the shape conjectured to attain it. Local optimality only, per secondary sources.
events.remains: Global optimality of the shape (the conjectured value), the exact value of the maximal area, and uniqueness.
events.time_since_posted: Not assessed for this pre-window event.
events.directly_checkable: The area of Gerver's sofa is checkable by hand or numerically; the Euler paper (2025) and Deng (2024) both reproduce about 2.2195 (see those events).
events.direction: Supports the value 2.2195 as the lower bound and conjectured maximum; does not prove optimality.
events.object: Gerver's sofa: an explicit planar shape built from 18 curve sections, area about 2.2195, and a rigid motion around the L-corner.

events.what_happened: D. Romik, 'Differential equations and exact solutions in the moving sofa problem', arXiv:1606.08111, v1 submitted 27 June 2016. Derives a family of six differential equations from the area-maximisation property, extending Gerver's approach; gives a closed-form candidate for the ambidextrous variant (sofa must turn left and right corners). Journal reference per secondary sources: Experimental Mathematics (2017 in one Wikipedia reference, 2018 in another); not verified.
events.revisions: v2 exists (per arXiv search results); journal version not verified.
events.delivers: Exact ODE characterisation of Gerver-type sofas, consistent with Gerver's local optimality. The closed-form shape answers the ambidextrous variant, not the one-corner problem.
events.remains: Global optimality of Gerver's shape, the exact value of the maximal area for the one-corner problem, and uniqueness.
events.time_since_posted: Not assessed for this pre-window event.
events.direction: Supports Gerver's shape as a critical point of the area functional; does not bound the maximum.
events.object: The ambidextrous candidate shape with area X + arctan Y, where X and Y solve x^2(x+3)=8 and x(4x^2+3)=1 (as reported in a search snippet of the abstract); the one-corner question is not the object here.

events.what_happened: Y. Kallus and D. Romik, 'Improved upper bounds in the moving sofa problem', arXiv:1706.06630, v1 submitted 21 June 2017 (later versions 29 Dec 2017, 5 Jan 2018, 11 Oct 2018); published Advances in Mathematics 340 (2018) 960-982 per Wikipedia. Abstract: 'We prove a new and improved upper bound of 2.37', by 'a computer-assisted proof scheme'.
events.revisions: v1 21 Jun 2017; v2 29 Dec 2017; v3 5 Jan 2018; v4 11 Oct 2018 (per arXiv abstract page).
events.delivers: Upper bound 2.37 on the maximal area (computer-assisted), reducing the gap to Gerver's 2.2195 from above.
events.remains: The exact value; the gap between about 2.2195 and 2.37 stays open until later upper bounds.
events.time_since_posted: Not assessed for this pre-window event.
events.doubts: The method is computer-assisted; the abstract says so, and the code (C++ with exact rational arithmetic, per a search snippet) was not opened.
events.direction: Moves an upper bound on the maximal area; does not settle the value.
events.object: No single object: a computer-assisted scheme giving an upper bound 2.37 on the maximal area.

events.what_happened: Jineon Baek (then University of Michigan), talk 'On the moving sofa problem', Department of Mathematics seminar, University of Pittsburgh, Thursday 8 February 2024 (seminar page). Abstract: 'Improving upon the computer-assisted approach of Kallus and Romik, we improve the upper bound to 2.32', and 'a conceptually new upper bound of 1 + pi^2/8 = 2.2337...', 'much closer to the lower bound of Gerver, on a large subset of shapes which includes Gerver's sofa'. No written argument for the 2.32 bound was found; the 2.2337 bound appeared in arXiv:2406.10725 (see baek-2024-06-conditional).
events.delivers: Announces an upper bound 2.32 on the maximal area (improving 2.37), and a conceptually new bound 2.2337 valid on a large subset of shapes that includes Gerver's sofa (the 2.2337 is conditional, see baek-2024-06-conditional).
events.remains: The exact value: the gap between Gerver's lower bound 2.2195 and the announced upper bound 2.32 stays open. Uniqueness and stability are not addressed.
events.doubts: The 2.32 bound is announced only in a seminar abstract. I did not find it stated as a result in the arXiv text I read (arXiv:2411.19826 HTML, read in full; arXiv:2406.10725 HTML, read in full). Whether it is certified, and by which method, is not established.
events.direction: Moves an upper bound on the maximal area; consistent with Gerver's value as the target.
events.object: No object: an upper-bound claim of 2.32 and a conditional bound 1 + pi^2/8 for shapes with an injectivity property.

events.what_happened: J. Baek, 'A Conditional Upper Bound for the Moving Sofa Problem', arXiv:2406.10725, v1 submitted 15 June 2024, math.MG. Models the problem as an infinite-dimensional convex quadratic optimisation. Theorem 1.2: a monotone sofa with rotation angle omega in (0, pi/2] satisfying the injectivity condition has area at most 1 + omega^2/2, so at most 1 + pi^2/8, about 2.2337. Conjecture 1.3 proposes that a maximum-area monotone sofa satisfies injectivity; if so, the paper gives an unconditional bound 1 + pi^2/8. The paper notes Gerver's sofa satisfies injectivity.
events.revisions: v1 15 Jun 2024 (per arXiv HTML); later versions not checked.
events.delivers: Conditional upper bound 1 + pi^2/8 (about 2.2337) on the area of monotone sofas satisfying the injectivity condition. Gerver's sofa satisfies that condition, so the bound is near Gerver's value, but it is not an unconditional bound on all sofas.
events.remains: The unconditional maximal area: the injectivity hypothesis (Conjecture 1.3) is not proved here, so the bound on all sofas is not established; the exact value remains open; uniqueness and stability are not addressed.
events.time_since_posted: About 16 months; no named expert engagement found.
events.direction: Upper bound conditional on an injectivity hypothesis; moves the maximal area bound only for the restricted class.
events.object: No object: an upper-bound argument for monotone sofas satisfying injectivity, by calculus of variations and Brunn-Minkowski theory; the paper says it does not rely on computer assistance.

events.what_happened: Z. Deng, 'Solving Moving Sofa Problem Using Calculus of Variations', arXiv:2407.02587, math.CA, v1 submitted 2 July 2024. Assumes convex trajectories and envelopes, solves the Euler-Lagrange equations numerically, obtains area about 2.2195316 (matching Gerver's sofa), and shows Gerver's sofa and Romik's car satisfy the Euler-Lagrange necessary condition for maximal area.
events.revisions: v1 2 Jul 2024 (abstract page); later versions not checked.
events.delivers: Numerical agreement with Gerver's area under an assumed convexity; shows the known shapes satisfy a necessary condition. Not a proof of optimality: the page claims no global optimality.
events.remains: Global optimality, exact value, uniqueness and stability.
events.time_since_posted: About 15 months; no named engagement found.
events.directly_checkable: The numerical area and Euler-Lagrange check can be reproduced from the paper's stated equations.
events.doubts: Relies on a convexity assumption on trajectories and envelopes; numerical; satisfying a necessary condition does not establish maximality.
events.direction: Consistency check on Gerver's shape; does not move the bound or the value.
events.object: Gerver's sofa and Romik's car, as numerical solutions of the Euler-Lagrange equations under convexity; explicit shapes.

events.what_happened: K. Leng, J. Bi, J. Cha, S. Pinilla, J. Thiyagalingam, 'Deep Learning Evidence for Global Optimality of Gerver's Sofa', arXiv:2407.11106 v1 submitted 15 July 2024; published Symmetry 16(10):1388 (accepted 16 Oct 2024, published 18 Oct 2024 per a search snippet of the journal page, which returned 403 to my fetch). Two neural-network methods: a continuous function learner with no assumption on monotonicity, symmetry or differentiability, and a discrete optimisation that improves the Kallus-Romik five-angle upper bound 'from 2.37 to 2.3337'. Training from many initialisations converges to Gerver's solution.
events.revisions: v1 15 Jul 2024; journal version Symmetry 16(10) 1388, Oct 2024.
events.delivers: Numerical evidence for global optimality of Gerver's sofa, and a numerical five-angle upper bound 2.3337 improving 2.37. Whether the 2.3337 is a certified bound is not established from what I read; the abstract reads as numerical.
events.remains: Global optimality (the paper describes it as evidence, not proof); the exact value; uniqueness.

checked_by.who: Referees of the journal Symmetry (MDPI); not named
checked_by.qualification: Anonymous journal referees; no named expert.
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the article for publication, 16 Oct 2024 (per journal page dates in a search snippet).

events.directly_checkable: The neural-network results are numerical and reproducible in principle; not checked by me.
events.doubts: Evidence for, not proof of, global optimality. The result is numerical, and the abstract as I read it does not state the 2.3337 bound is certified.
events.direction: Supports Gerver's shape as the optimum; moves a numerical upper-bound estimate for five angles from 2.37 to 2.3337.
events.object: Numerically found sofa shapes converging to Gerver's shape; a five-angle discretised upper bound of 2.3337. Explicit numerical objects, not a proof.

events.what_happened: J. Baek, 'Optimality of Gerver's Sofa', arXiv:2411.19826, v1 submitted 29 Nov 2024 16:37 UTC; 119 pages, 21 figures; math.MG, with math.CO and math.OC; no affiliation on the arXiv page (Yonsei University at posting per press). The abstract: 'We resolve the moving sofa problem by showing that Gerver's construction with 18 curve sections attains the maximum area' (2.2195...). Theorem 1.1.1: 'Gerver's sofa G attains the maximum area alpha_max of a moving sofa.' The paper says 'The proof does not require computer assistance, except for numerical computations that can be done on a scientific calculator.' The acknowledgements say a prior version of the proof was computer-assisted and the MovingSofas software 'does not appear in the final proof'. Press (Quanta, Feb 2025; ScienceAlert, Dec 2024) reports it as the claimed resolution; Wikipedia cites it as a 119-page preprint claiming Gerver's value is optimal, 'which if true would solve the moving sofa problem'.
events.revisions: v1 only (29 Nov 2024). The arXiv abstract page as read on 13 Oct 2026 lists no later version; the Kingy tracker (checked 29 Jul 2026) also shows only the original version.
events.delivers: Claims the maximal area of a planar moving sofa through the unit-width L-corridor equals the area of Gerver's sofa, about 2.2195, which would give the exact value of the sofa constant. Restricted to the planar one-corner problem as stated; does not claim uniqueness (Theorem 1.1.1 does not use 'unique'; the word appears only in Proposition 1.2.1 about translations in standard position).
events.remains: Nothing in problem_asks is left open if the proof holds: the value, and the fact that Gerver's sofa attains it. Not asked and still open: whether the maximiser is unique (the bullet does not ask), and stability. Whether the proof is correct is not yet established by any named human reading.

checked_by.qualification: Automated AI referee; not a human mathematician.
checked_by.what_they_did: Review dated 12 Aug 2026 calls the paper 'a serious, largely self-contained claim to have resolved the moving sofa problem', finds the logic coherent, and gives the verdict 'the appropriate verdict is conditional, not accept'. Caveats: 'no formal verification' and 'black-box dependence on the same circle of results'; flags the citation of Gerver's Theorem 2 for Theorem 6.1.2 (with a connectedness gap in Gerver's balancing argument) and Remark 6.1.1's unverified inequalities. States 'No human expert has reviewed it yet.'

checked_by.who: Automated audit (baek/REPORT.md) in the vltanh/lean4-moving-sofa repository; the README credits Claude Opus 5.5 with writing the audit
checked_by.qualification: AI-written audit of the paper's argument against its Lean formalisation; not a human reading.
checked_by.what_they_did: Lists errors E6 (Definition 3.2.5 uses parallelogram P_omega where fan F_omega is meant), E11 ('the direction (1) => (2) of Proposition 5.1.4 is false'), and gaps E12 (proof of Theorem 6.1.2 'rests on a misreading of Gerver's Theorem 2'), E21 (use of N(K) subset K, which the cap space does not provide), E24 (Theorem 8.4.1 'stated without proof'); says 'Every result of the paper survives with the intended statements.'

events.time_since_posted: About 22 months to 13 Oct 2026; no journal publication found (Kingy, 29 Jul 2026); no named human verification found in any source I opened.

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 with Mathlib (three independent formalisations; see events deancureton-2026-09, ruifengcao-2026-09, vltanh-2026-10-formalisation)

events.directly_checkable: The sofa Gerver describes is explicit and its area (about 2.2195) can be reproduced numerically (see deng-2024-07 and the 2025 Euler paper); the optimality claim itself is not checkable by hand.
events.doubts: (1) No named human has verified the argument in public; press reports 'a broad consensus' and 'initial comments ... optimistic' from unnamed mathematicians. (2) Author's own statements of gaps: Section 1.7.2 says the paper '(essentially) prove[s]' a weaker inequality; Section 1.3.2 says Gerver's balancing argument 'has a subtle logical gap that does not address the connectedness of moving sofas'. (3) The formalisations report errors and gaps in the paper, listed in checked_by and events deancureton-2026-09 and vltanh-2026-10-formalisation. Those were repaired in the Lean development, and the formalisers report that the main theorem survives; the Pith referee flags Theorem 6.1.2 and Remark 6.1.1 as load-bearing and not yet independently checked. (4) The 'Annals of Mathematics' review claimed in a Korea Herald piece (4 Jan 2026) is press-only; Kingy found no journal publication at 29 Jul 2026. (5) Earlier computer-assisted versions of the proof existed (acknowledgements).
events.direction: Asserts the conjectured value: Gerver's 2.2195 is the maximal area. It answers the bullet's 'what is the largest area' with a value, and is not a counterexample.
events.object: Gerver's sofa: an explicit planar moving sofa built from 18 curve sections (per the abstract), with area about 2.2195 (Theorem 1.1.1 says it attains the maximum). The object is explicit; the maximality claim rests on the paper's proof, not on a non-constructive existence argument.

events.what_happened: google-deepmind/formal-conjectures, FormalConjectures/Wikipedia/MovingSofa.lean. The file defines the sofa constant ('the maximal area of a moving sofa'), tags 'What is the sofa constant?' as 'research solved', states 'theorem sofaConstant_eq : sofaConstant = answer(volume gerversSofa)', and says 'Gerver's sofa attains the sofa constant, conjectured by [Ge92] and claimed by [Ba24]', also tagged research solved. Its Lean theorems are proved by sorry in this file; the 'research solved' tags rest on external formal proofs linked with commit hashes but no dates. The header reads 'Copyright 2026'.
events.revisions: Not established; the file header shows only the 2026 copyright.
events.delivers: A status classification, not a mathematical result: it records the sofa constant as solved and equal to the area of Gerver's sofa, citing Baek's claim, and records the external formal proofs as the support.
events.remains: Per the vltanh README, the upstream file lists uniqueness of the optimal sofa as open. The file does not itself prove any of the three theorems.
events.doubts: The file's own theorems are sorry-stubs; the 'research solved' label depends on the external repositories it links, which I could not date.
events.direction: Records Gerver's sofa as the optimum, citing Baek's claim; consistent with the claimed value.

events.what_happened: Mathematical exploration and discovery at scale, arXiv:2511.02864, v1 submitted 3 Nov 2025 (latest revision 22 Dec 2025 per abstract page). The paper tests the AlphaEvolve system on 67 problems and has a section 'Moving sofa problem' (the table of contents lists '42 Moving sofa problem' in Section 6; a search snippet names problems 6.62 and 6.63). I could not read the sofa section: the HTML and ar5iv copies are truncated before it and the PDF exceeds the fetch size limit. A search snippet (secondary, unverified) reports that AlphaEvolve approximates Gerver's sofa within 0.02% and Romik's variant within 1.5%, recovering known shapes, and a 3D sofa analogue of volume at least 1.81 (estimated 1.84) that the authors 'believe' is larger than prior constructions.
events.revisions: v1 3 Nov 2025; latest revision 22 Dec 2025 (abstract page).
events.delivers: Unverified from the primary text. As reported secondarily: recovery of Gerver's and Romik's 2D sofas to small error (no improvement on 2.2195), and a 3D analogue construction. The 3D analogue is a different question from the planar bullet.
events.remains: Unverified from the primary text. As reported: the planar sofa constant remains open in the paper's own treatment; the 3D problem is outside the bullet.
events.doubts: The sofa section was not read; the search-snippet summary may misstate the numbers or the 'believe' claim. The author names in 'people' also come from a search snippet, not from the paper. Treat as unverified.
events.direction: As reported secondarily: recovers known 2D shapes (cuts toward Gerver's value, not beyond it) and gives a 3D analogue (different question). Not verified.
events.object: As reported secondarily: AlphaEvolve-found planar sofa approximations to Gerver's and Romik's shapes, and a 3D sofa analogue. Not verified from the paper.

events.what_happened: deancureton/MovingSofa, GitHub repository: 'This repository contains a Lean 4 proof that Gerver's sofa has the largest area of any shape that can be moved around a right-angled corner in a hallway of width one.' Main theorem: MovingSofa.sofaConstant_eq_volume_gerversSofa : sofaConstant = volume gerversSofa, 'the Theorem 1.1 of the paper'. Commits: 'formalize the optimality of gerver's sofa' (20 Sep 2026) and a second commit on 22 Sep 2026. The README says: 'The proof is about 66,000 lines of Lean, not counting dependencies. It was written in about four days by AI coding agents (OpenAI Codex and Claude Code), directed by Dean Cureton.' It also says: 'Formalizing the paper surfaced 11 small errors/gaps in the paper's proofs, and 33 misprints. These are all repaired here, and none of them break the main theorem.' The area of Gerver's sofa is 'only shown to be' at least 11/5; the value 2.2195 is not checked.
events.revisions: Two commits (20 and 22 Sep 2026); no release listed.
events.delivers: A Lean 4 formalisation of Baek's optimality theorem, with the main theorem stated as above, checked by Comparator with a nanoda kernel replay. Restricted to Baek's statement; it does not check that the area value 2.2195 is correct beyond the lower bound 11/5 (the README says the decimal value is unchecked). The README says it proves three theorems that Baek's paper imports or leaves unproved, for the upstream gerversSofa.
events.remains: Uniqueness and stability are not claimed by this repository. The 2.2195 decimal is not checked in Lean.

events.what_happened: RuifengCao/sofa-formal, GitHub repository: 'Lean 4 proof that Gerver's sofa has the maximal area (moving sofa problem)'. It states the main theorem sofaConstant_eq_volume_gerversSofa, formalising Baek's paper (arXiv:2411.19826v1). Versions Lean v4.33.1 and Mathlib v4.33.1, matching formal-conjectures. Per the README (as fetched): 'No sorry is used, and no axioms beyond Lean's standard three'; the only sorry warnings are in Challenge.lean statement files. The repository says Baek imports Theorems 6.1.2 and 8.4.2 and leaves Theorem 8.4.1 unproved, and that the repository proves all three for the upstream gerversSofa. Uniqueness is marked 'open; Baek does not claim it.' Status stamp 'round 42' dated 23 Sep 2026; release v1.0.0 at commit 838baca, undated. The README names no author and no AI system.

events.doubts: Only the README was read; the repository has two commits and no visible author. The README says the constants are checked by 'kernel-checked interval arithmetic'. Lean kernel checks do not verify that the definitions match the intended meaning.

(2) Lean's kernel 'checks the proofs, not that the statements mean what you intend'. (3) The audit lists errors E6 (Definition 3.2.5 uses the parallelogram P_omega where the fan F_omega is meant), E11 (one direction of Proposition 5.1.4 is false), and gaps E12 (the proof of Theorem 6.1.2 'rests on a misreading of Gerver's Theorem 2'), E21 (use of N(K) subset K, which the cap space does not provide), E24 (Theorem 8.4.1, the structure of Gerver's sofa, 'stated without proof'), plus slips and minor gaps; the audit says the claims hold nevertheless. The formalisation and audit are both AI-written.

events.what_happened: In the same repository (vltanh/lean4-moving-sofa), the README claims three further results beyond Baek's paper: (a) uniqueness: Gerver's sofa 'is the only optimal sofa, up to rigid motions'; the README says 'Baek's paper does not prove this, and Google DeepMind's formal-conjectures lists it as open'; (b) stability: a sofa whose area is epsilon less is within Hausdorff distance C sqrt(epsilon) of Gerver's sofa, with exponent 1/2 not improvable; (c) a 'coercive certificate': 'A single estimate for Baek's upper bound, the coercive certificate, proves optimality and uniqueness again', and 'the stability proof rests on it'. The README says: 'ChatGPT Pro 6 wrote the arguments for uniqueness, stability and the certificate for this repository; they have not been peer reviewed.' CREDITS says ChatGPT Pro 6 (OpenAI) wrote the informal uniqueness argument and uncompiled Lean drafts; Claude Opus 5.5 checked the drafts, replaced the 54 proofs that did not compile with sorry, then proved them again. The uniqueness round ran from 2 Oct 2026, and the connection with formal-conjectures on 2-3 Oct.
events.revisions: Uniqueness and stability rounds ran 2-7 Oct 2026 (CREDITS); the repository is at version 5 at the last round.
events.delivers: Claimed (AI-written, not peer reviewed, Lean-checked in the repository): uniqueness of Gerver's sofa up to rigid motions as the unique optimal sofa; a stability estimate (area deficit epsilon implies Hausdorff distance C sqrt(epsilon)); and a route to optimality and uniqueness via the certificate, 'without Baek's Theorem 1.1.1'. The certificate route is a second proof of optimality, not Baek's; the README says Baek's paper does not cover uniqueness or the stability and certificate results.
events.remains: None of problem_asks is left open by these results, since the bullet asks only for the value. Their status as proofs rests on the Lean checks and on the unreviewed AI-written arguments. The README says Baek's paper does not prove uniqueness and that formal-conjectures lists it as open.

events.what_happened: O. Mushkarov and N. Nikolov, 'Moving rectangular sofas in planar and spatial corridors', arXiv:2604.01174, v1 submitted 1 April 2026, math.MG. Abstract: 'We consider eight natural planar corridors, including the standard L-shaped one, and characterize the rectangles that can move around their corners. As a bi-product we describe completely the corresponding rectangles with maximum area, as well as the rectangular parallelepipeds with maximum volume that can move around the corners of the spatial analogues of the considered eight planar corridors.'
events.delivers: Results on rectangles in eight corridors (including the L-corridor) and on 3D analogues. This is a restricted class (rectangles, not general shapes), so it settles nothing about the maximal area over all sofas.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, for the general-shape problem; the paper does not address it on the abstract I read.
events.direction: Neighbouring question (rectangles, multiple corridors); not an answer to the bullet.
events.object: Rectangles of maximal area through the L-corridor and other corridors; not a counterexample to any claim about general sofas.

events.what_happened: X. He, 'A Gas-Driven Algorithm for Variants of the Moving Sofa Problem', arXiv:2608.11206. The abstract page says 'Submitted on 8 Apr 2026' (v1), though the identifier 2608 would normally indicate August 2026; I could not resolve this. Abstract: a numerical algorithm based on a gas-pressure-driven dynamical system; 'Numerical experiments show that the method effectively approximates the known Gerver's sofa result, and provides numerical estimates of the possible maximum area for corridors with different angles'; a motion-pattern intersection at 43.327 degrees where the locally maximal sofa area is 1.8674.
events.revisions: v1 (date conflict with identifier; see doubts).
events.delivers: Numerical estimates for variant corridors with different angles, and an approximation to Gerver's sofa. Not an unconditional bound on the L-corridor problem as stated; it is a variant.
events.remains: All of problem_asks for the unit-width right-angle corridor; the paper gives no rigorous bound on it from the abstract.
events.time_since_posted: Unclear: the date is in conflict with the identifier.
events.doubts: Numerical; variants with different corridor angles; the arXiv identifier and the submitted date disagree. Only the abstract page was read.
events.direction: Neighbouring variant (corridor angles); numerical; does not settle the one-corner question.
events.object: A numerically computed locally maximal sofa of area 1.8674 at a corridor angle of 43.327 degrees; not explicit beyond the numbers in the abstract.

disputes.summary: Publication status of Baek's claim is reported inconsistently. The Korea Herald piece (4 Jan 2026) says the paper is 'now under review at Annals of Mathematics'; Quanta (14 Feb 2025) says 'still being peer-reviewed'; Kingy (checked 29 Jul 2026) found 'No journal publication ... located' and 'Peer reviewed: No'; the Pith referee (12 Aug 2026) says 'No human expert has reviewed it yet'. The Annals claim rests on press alone and I could not confirm it.

The google-deepmind formal-conjectures file tags the sofa constant and Gerver's optimality as 'research solved' and cites Baek's claim, while its theorems are sorry-stubs. Per the vltanh README, the same upstream file lists uniqueness of the optimal sofa as open. The formal-conjectures labels rest on external repositories I could not date.

Baek's paper is a claim about the maximal area only. The RuifengCao README says Baek 'does not claim' uniqueness; the vltanh README says the uniqueness and stability results are AI-written and not in Baek's paper. Whether AI-written uniqueness work bears on this bullet's question is for the judging pass; the bullet asks only for the value.

summary: Baek's preprint (arXiv:2411.19826, v1 29 Nov 2024; still only v1 as of 13 Oct 2026 on the abstract page) claims that Gerver's 1992 sofa, area about 2.2195, is the maximal-area planar moving sofa through the unit-width L-corridor. Its Theorem 1.1.1 says 'Gerver's sofa G attains the maximum area alpha_max of a moving sofa'. I read the arXiv HTML version in full (the PDF text did not extract); it names no AI system and says the proof 'does not require computer assistance, except for numerical computations that can be done on a scientific calculator'; its acknowledgements say an earlier version was computer-assisted. Press coverage (ScienceAlert 12 Dec 2024; Quanta 14 Feb 2025; Scientific American via a Feb 2025 article; Korea Herald 4 Jan 2026) reports the claim as a resolution while stating it is 'yet to be peer-reviewed'. I found no named human who has publicly verified the argument: Quanta quotes Michael Zieve, Baek's adviser, praising the no-computer approach but describes no check; Scientific American and KIAS cite unnamed 'mathematicians who know Baek' and a 'broad consensus'. The Pith AI referee (deepseek-v4-flash, 12 Aug 2026) gives the verdict 'conditional, not accept', citing reliance on Gerver's Theorem 2 for Theorem 6.1.2 and an unverified inequality in Remark 6.1.1. Three Lean 4 formalisations of the paper appeared in Sep-Oct 2026: deancureton/MovingSofa (commits 20-22 Sep 2026; 'written in about four days by AI coding agents (OpenAI Codex and Claude Code)'; reports '11 small errors/gaps in the paper's proofs, and 33 misprints', all repaired, none breaking the main theorem); RuifengCao/sofa-formal (status stamp 23 Sep 2026; README names no AI and no author; reports Baek imports Theorems 6.1.2 and 8.4.2 and leaves 8.4.1 unproved, all three proved in the repository); and vltanh/lean4-moving-sofa (formalisation 1-2 Oct 2026, with an AI-written audit listing E6 and E11 (a false direction of Proposition 5.1.4), gaps E12 (a 'misreading of Gerver's Theorem 2' for Theorem 6.1.2), E21 and E24, and the claim that 'Every result of the paper survives with the intended statements'). The vltanh repository also credits AI-written arguments for uniqueness, stability and a 'coercive certificate' that it says reprove optimality and uniqueness without Baek's Theorem 1.1.1; these are not peer reviewed, and uniqueness is not asked by the bullet. Earlier and related events are all numerical or bounds: Hammersley 1968 (lower 2.2074, upper 2sqrt2), Gerver 1992 (2.2195), Romik 2016, Kallus-Romik 2017 (upper 2.37, computer-assisted), Baek's Feb 2024 talk announcing an upper bound 2.32, Baek's June 2024 conditional bound 1+pi^2/8 = 2.2337 (conditional on an injectivity hypothesis), Deng July 2024 (numerical Euler-Lagrange, no optimality claim), and Leng et al. July 2024 (neural-network evidence; five-angle upper bound 2.37 to 2.3337, numerical). AI search: I found no AI-produced counterexample and no AI-produced optimality argument other than the vltanh uniqueness/certificate work and the formalisation credits. The AlphaEvolve paper (arXiv:2511.02864) has a 'Moving sofa problem' section that I could not read; a search snippet reports that it recovers Gerver's and Romik's shapes and gives a 3D analogue, which I have not verified. Close calls: (1) whether the uniqueness/stability/certificate arguments belong to this bullet (the bullet asks only for the value); (2) whether the AI-coded repairs in the two formalisations are load-bearing mathematics, or only formalisation; (3) whether Leng et al.'s 2.3337 is a certified bound that moves the quantity (the abstract reads as numerical); (4) whether Baek's 2.32 bound from the 2024 talk appears in the paper (I did not find it in the text I read).
competing_reading: The strongest case for a resolution: the main claim is a single theorem about one quantity, and three independent Lean 4 formalisations with kernel checks, comparator replay and a stated 'Lean kernel' check now support the statement, with the errors reported in the paper repaired and the main theorem surviving by each formaliser's account. The AI-written parts are checks and extensions, not the main argument. Under that reading the problem's value is determined, subject only to the formal statements matching the intended problem. The strongest case against: no named human has read the argument in public after 22 months; the two AI-credited formalisations and the AI audit are the only detailed readings, and they are by people or agents with a stake in the formal result; the paper itself admits that its key steps are 'essentially' proved for a weaker inequality (Section 1.7.2) and that Gerver's balancing argument has a gap (Section 1.3.2); the audit lists a false direction of Proposition 5.1.4 and a load-bearing misreading of Gerver's Theorem 2 for Theorem 6.1.2; the AI referee calls it conditional, not accept; and Lean kernel checks do not verify that the definitions match the problem.
what_would_settle_it: A journal acceptance (Annals of Mathematics is claimed by press but not confirmed), or a named expert's written verification of the balancing step and of Theorem 6.1.2 (the Gerver Theorem 2 citation), with the audit's E11 (Proposition 5.1.4) and E12 resolved by the author or referees. For the AI question: the authors' own acknowledgement of any AI tool in the paper (the PDF text was not readable, so the arXiv HTML is the only text I could read in full), and the AlphaEvolve paper's sofa section (2511.02864), which I could not read. Also the Palomar registry entry PALOMAR-2026-10-02-000008 (not loadable here), and the first commit dates of the three formalisation repositories.

event.what_happened: J. Baek, 'Optimality of Gerver's Sofa', arXiv:2411.19826, v1 submitted 29 Nov 2024 16:37 UTC; 119 pages, 21 figures; math.MG, with math.CO and math.OC; no affiliation on the arXiv page (Yonsei University at posting per press). The abstract: 'We resolve the moving sofa problem by showing that Gerver's construction with 18 curve sections attains the maximum area' (2.2195...). Theorem 1.1.1: 'Gerver's sofa G attains the maximum area alpha_max of a moving sofa.' The paper says 'The proof does not require computer assistance, except for numerical computations that can be done on a scientific calculator.' The acknowledgements say a prior version of the proof was computer-assisted and the MovingSofas software 'does not appear in the final proof'. Press (Quanta, Feb 2025; ScienceAlert, Dec 2024) reports it as the claimed resolution; Wikipedia cites it as a 119-page preprint claiming Gerver's value is optimal, 'which if true would solve the moving sofa problem'.
event.revisions: v1 only (29 Nov 2024). The arXiv abstract page as read on 13 Oct 2026 lists no later version; the Kingy tracker (checked 29 Jul 2026) also shows only the original version.
event.delivers: Claims the maximal area of a planar moving sofa through the unit-width L-corridor equals the area of Gerver's sofa, about 2.2195, which would give the exact value of the sofa constant. Restricted to the planar one-corner problem as stated; does not claim uniqueness (Theorem 1.1.1 does not use 'unique'; the word appears only in Proposition 1.2.1 about translations in standard position).
event.remains: Nothing in problem_asks is left open if the proof holds: the value, and the fact that Gerver's sofa attains it. Not asked and still open: whether the maximiser is unique (the bullet does not ask), and stability. Whether the proof is correct is not yet established by any named human reading.

checked_by.qualification: Automated AI referee; not a human mathematician.
checked_by.what_they_did: Review dated 12 Aug 2026 calls the paper 'a serious, largely self-contained claim to have resolved the moving sofa problem', finds the logic coherent, and gives the verdict 'the appropriate verdict is conditional, not accept'. Caveats: 'no formal verification' and 'black-box dependence on the same circle of results'; flags the citation of Gerver's Theorem 2 for Theorem 6.1.2 (with a connectedness gap in Gerver's balancing argument) and Remark 6.1.1's unverified inequalities. States 'No human expert has reviewed it yet.'

event.directly_checkable: The sofa Gerver describes is explicit and its area (about 2.2195) can be reproduced numerically (see deng-2024-07 and the 2025 Euler paper); the optimality claim itself is not checkable by hand.
event.doubts: (1) No named human has verified the argument in public; press reports 'a broad consensus' and 'initial comments ... optimistic' from unnamed mathematicians. (2) Author's own statements of gaps: Section 1.7.2 says the paper '(essentially) prove[s]' a weaker inequality; Section 1.3.2 says Gerver's balancing argument 'has a subtle logical gap that does not address the connectedness of moving sofas'. (3) The formalisations report errors and gaps in the paper, listed in checked_by and events deancureton-2026-09 and vltanh-2026-10-formalisation. Those were repaired in the Lean development, and the formalisers report that the main theorem survives; the Pith referee flags Theorem 6.1.2 and Remark 6.1.1 as load-bearing and not yet independently checked. (4) The 'Annals of Mathematics' review claimed in a Korea Herald piece (4 Jan 2026) is press-only; Kingy found no journal publication at 29 Jul 2026. (5) Earlier computer-assisted versions of the proof existed (acknowledgements).
event.direction: Asserts the conjectured value: Gerver's 2.2195 is the maximal area. It answers the bullet's 'what is the largest area' with a value, and is not a counterexample.
event.object: Gerver's sofa: an explicit planar moving sofa built from 18 curve sections (per the abstract), with area about 2.2195 (Theorem 1.1.1 says it attains the maximum). The object is explicit; the maximality claim rests on the paper's proof, not on a non-constructive existence argument.

events.credibility_reason: The 2.32 upper bound exists only as a seminar abstract; no written argument for it was found, including in Baek's later preprints.
The 2.3337 five-angle figure reads as a numerical estimate rather than a certified bound; the paper presents itself as evidence, not proof.

No named human has verified it after ~22 months; the author concedes a connectedness gap in Gerver's balancing argument; an AI audit reports a false direction of Prop. 5.1.4 and a misreading of Gerver's Theorem 2 underlying Thm 6.1.2, which the formalisers say they repaired without the main theorem breaking. These are doubts but not unanswered errors, so it is not knocked down.
The sofa section was never read; the content comes only from a search snippet. As reported, it recovers known planar shapes and adds a 3D analogue, which is a different question.
The arguments are AI-written and checked only by Lean; the README says no person has reviewed the proofs, statements or definitions.
events.ai_basis: ChatGPT Pro 6 wrote the arguments for uniqueness, stability and the certificate for this repository; they have not been peer reviewed.

events.credibility_reason: The arXiv identifier and the submission date disagree, and the results are numerical only.

judgement.why: The statement asks only for the maximal area. Baek's preprint determines that value (Gerver's sofa attains it), so its scope is whole and Gerver's sofa is a witness. Its verification is unreviewed: no named human has read it, the formal-conjectures tag cites it without checking it, and three Lean builds plus an AI audit and an AI referee are formal or automated checks, not digestion (F7, F8). I marked it doubtful rather than credible because of the author's own admitted gap and the audit's specific errors. Those errors are reported repaired, so it is not knocked down. The three formalisations are scope none with ai_role none, because the AI only formalised and audited an argument a human had already proved. The vltanh uniqueness/stability event is a stronger form of the question, so it is a variant. Its 'coercive certificate' is said to reprove optimality, but it sits inside Baek's framework, has no human reading, and the record cannot show it is an independent answer. Its AI role is generated (ChatGPT Pro 6 wrote the arguments), but that credit belongs to the variant event only. Baek's 2024-06 bound is conditional on an unproven injectivity conjecture, so it is a reduction and scored none. Leng et al. is numerical evidence with an uncertified bound, so none. Hammersley, Gerver and Kallus-Romik are pre-snapshot bounds. Romik 2016's closed form answers the ambidextrous variant.
judgement.doubts: Close call: whether the vltanh 'coercive certificate' is a second, AI-generated whole answer to the value. If it is, it would tie Baek at the top tier and pass an AI 'generated' role to the problem. I read it as a variant/extension because the record describes it only through the README and it relies on Baek's framework. Baek's own 2.32 talk bound has no written argument. The AlphaEvolve sofa section was never read.
judgement.by: judging pass (JUDGE.md), claude-opus-5-5; not the researching agent and not a human reviewer
